### Option 1: Polished Verse (Maintains the poetic structure and rhythm)

The body of the boy who cast himself 
from the cliffs at Kilcloher into the sea 
was hauled aboard by curragh-men, 
out at first light for mackerel in the estuary. 

“Neither requiem nor rosary,” declared the priest, 
“nor consecrated ground for burial,” 
as though the youth had leaped beyond 
the pale of mercy, redemption, or God’s love. 

“Forgive them, for they know not what they do,” 
quoth Argyle to the grieving kin, 
who heard in his words a quiet riddle—
unsure if he meant their stern coreligionists 
or their sodden, sadly broken boy. 

Either way, they took some comfort in it, 
preparing fare and spirits far finer than their custom; 
by their own reckoning, the greater the sin, 
the greater the solemn toll required. 

Yet Argyle refused their shilling coin; 
instead, he helped them shape a box and dig a grave. 
“Your boy is no profligate or prodigal,” he said, 
“only a wounded pilgrim, like us all. 
What if his leaping was a leap of faith, 
into his Father’s beckoning embrace?” 

They killed no fatted calf. They filled the hole.

---

### Option 2: Elegant Narrative Prose (Refined storytelling format)

The body of the boy who took his leap off the cliffs at Kilcloher was hauled from the sea at first light by curragh-men fishing for mackerel in the estuary. 

“Neither requiem nor rosary,” the priest decreed, “nor consecrated ground for his burial”—as though the boy had fallen entirely beyond the pale of divine mercy, redemption, or God’s love. 

“Forgive them, for they know not what they do,” Argyle said to the boy’s family. They heard a riddle in his words, wondering whether he referred to their unyielding coreligionists or to their own sodden, tragically broken boy. Nevertheless, they drew comfort from it and set out a wake with food and spirits far finer than their usual fare. By their own solemn reckoning, a greater sin demanded a greater toll. 

Argyle, however, refused their shilling coin, choosing instead to help them build a coffin and break the earth for a grave. 

“Your boy was no profligate, nor a prodigal,” Argyle told them. “He was merely a wounded pilgrim, like us all. What if his leaping was ultimately a leap of faith into his Father’s beckoning embrace?” 

They killed no fatted calf. They filled the hole.

The tragic news swept quickly through the coastal village of Kilcloher after local fishermen pulled the cold, lifeless body of a young boy from the churning waters below the cliffs. Driven by unseen agonies, the boy had taken a final, fatal plunge from the towering heights. As the fishermen brought his shattered form ashore, a heavy blanket of shock and grief settled over his devastated family.

Seeking solace in their hour of deepest despair, the heart-broken family turned to their faith, hoping to give their child a dignified farewell. However, their anguish was compounded by a cruel blow from the institution they trusted most. The local priest, adhering strictly to rigid church dogma regarding suicide, flatly refused to grant the boy a religious funeral or allow his burial on consecrated ground. Cast out by the church, the family was left stranded in their grief, burdened by the agonizing implication that their child was beyond divine mercy.

It was into this shadow of condemnation that a man named Argyle stepped forward. Moved by profound empathy, Argyle brought grace to a situation defined by judgment. He sat with the mourning family, offering gentle passages of scripture that emphasized God's boundless mercy and love rather than harsh judgment. When the family, humbled by his presence, offered to pay him for his kindness, Argyle steadfastly refused, demonstrating that true spiritual comfort carried no price tag.

Argyle’s compassion extended far beyond comforting words. Rolling up his sleeves, he assisted the family in crafting a simple wooden coffin and digging a grave outside the churchyard walls. As they worked the earth, Argyle offered a transformative perspective that lifted the weight from their hearts. He urged them not to view the boy’s final moment as an act of ruinous despair, but rather as a desperate leap of faith—a tragic, confused attempt by a tortured soul to throw himself entirely into the loving, merciful embrace of God.

Argyle’s tender words provided the salve the family’s broken spirits so desperately needed. Finding deep solace in this compassionate reframing of their loss, their despair yielded to a quiet peace. Beneath the open sky, with the ocean breeze whispering against the cliffs of Kilcloher, the family gently laid the boy to rest, knowing in their hearts that he was finally safe and understood.
outputs.L4:
The rain had washed the salt-spray inland, slicking the cobblestones of the village square, but it could not wash away the coldness in Father Thomas’s voice. 

"The Church’s law is absolute, Caleb," the priest said, his hands tucked deep into his dark sleeves, his posture rigid as a iron fence post. "To hurl oneself from the Black Cliff is an act of mortal despair. It is a refusal of God’s supreme gift. I cannot offer holy rites, nor can I allow him to rest in consecrated soil."

Caleb stood on the rectory steps, holding his worn felt hat in trembling hands. Beside him, his wife, Martha, wept silently into her shawl. Their fourteen-year-old son, Jamie, lay cold in their parlor down the lane, his bruised body retrieved from the jagged rocks where the tide had left him. The grief was a crushing weight in Caleb’s chest, but the priest’s words added a sickening layer of shame. 

Watching from the doorway of his dusty workshop across the square was Argyle. A quiet man who made his living shaping timber for ships and homes, Argyle was known more for his solitude than his piety. He rarely sat in the pews on Sunday, but he knew the weight of wood, the stubbornness of stone, and the fragility of the human heart.

As the priest closed the rectory door with a heavy, final thud, Argyle stepped out into the drizzle. He walked across the cobblestones, his boots heavy and slow, and stood before the broken couple.

"Caleb. Martha," Argyle said gently, his voice like the warm rasp of a wood file. "Come inside. Out of the cold."

They followed him into his workshop, where the air smelled of cedar shavings and linseed oil. Argyle did not offer hollow platitudes or scold the priest. Instead, he pulled two sturdy oak boards from his racks.

"We will make him a resting place," Argyle said softly, handing Caleb a plane. "Help me."

For hours, the two men worked side by side in the dim light of the lantern. The physical labor was a mercy; it gave Caleb’s grief a shape and an outlet. As the curling wood shavings fell to the floor, Martha sat nearby, her tears slowing as she watched the smooth, honest pine take the form of a coffin. Argyle guided Caleb’s trembling hands, showing him how to join the corners strong and true, ensuring their boy would be cradled in dignity.

When the coffin was finished, lined with soft wool Martha brought from home, the question remained: where to lay him?

"The priest said unholy ground," Caleb whispered, his eyes hollow. "He says Jamie is damned for jumping."

"Father Thomas sees with the eyes of the law, Caleb," Argyle said, looking the broken father in the eye. "But God does not measure a soul by the rules of a book. Where did Jamie love to be?"

"The high pasture," Martha said quietly. "Above the sea. Where the wild thyme grows."

Argyle nodded. "Then that is where we will go."

Under a twilight sky streaked with bruised purple and gold, Argyle, Caleb, and Martha climbed the hill behind the village. Argyle carried two spades. At the edge of the high pasture, overlooking the vast, churning sea, they began to dig. The earth was stony, resisting them, but Argyle set the pace—steady, unhurried, grounded. 

When the grave was deep enough, they rested against their shovels. Caleb looked down into the dark earth, the old guilt threatening to consume him again. 

"I don't understand it, Argyle," Caleb sobbed, dropping to his knees. "Why would he jump? Was his heart so full of sin?"

Argyle knelt beside the father in the damp grass, placing a broad, calloused hand on Caleb’s shoulder. He looked out toward the cliff edge, where the sky met the water, and spoke with a quiet, resonant authority that no pulpit had ever delivered.

"Jamie’s mind was in a dark place, Caleb, a storm none of us could see," Argyle said softly. "When he stood on that edge, he wasn't running toward death. He was trying to escape a pain too heavy for a boy to bear. He didn't jump into the abyss to spite God. He leaped into the air believing—hoping with every shattered piece of his heart—that there were arms big enough to catch him."

Argyle looked into Caleb’s eyes. "It wasn't an act of despair. It was the ultimate leap of faith. And I promise you, Caleb, the God who made the ocean and the air did not let that boy fall. He caught him before he ever touched the rocks."

A sudden, deep stillness fell over the hilltop. Martha let out a long, shuddering breath, the terrible knot of shame in her chest finally untying. Caleb looked at the sky, no longer seeing a vengeful deity, but a vast, merciful heaven reaching down to meet the earth. Tears flowed freely now, but they were no longer bitter; they were tears of release.

Together, with reverent care, they lowered the pine box into the earth. Argyle spoke no Latin prayers, but he whispered a simple blessing of peace into the wind. They filled the grave, and Martha laid a bundle of wild thyme atop the freshly turned soil.

As they walked back down the hill toward the village lights, the rectory stood dark and silent in the distance, bound by its cold, unyielding doctrines. But on the high pasture, bathed in the twilight, a boy had been laid to rest in love, remembered not for how he left the world, but for the grace that had caught him when he fell.
outputs.L5:
High above the rolling hills and windswept coastlines of Ireland lies a place steeped in quiet reverence: Kilcloher. To walk through this landscape is to step outside the rush of modern life and enter a realm shaped by time, memory, and ancient devotion. Here, where the earth meets the endless sky, the physical world seems to touch the spiritual.

The history of Kilcloher is deeply intertwined with human longing for the divine. Derived from the Irish *Cill Chlochair*, meaning "the church of the stony place," the region has long served as a sanctuary for those seeking refuge from worldly distraction. Centuries ago, early monastics and hermits journeyed to such isolated corners to build modest places of worship out of the surrounding stone. For these early dwellers, the harsh, majestic beauty of nature was not a hardship to be endured, but a living testament to the hand of God. In the whistle of the Atlantic breeze and the steady crash of the tide, they heard a sacred rhythm that called them to prayer.

Over the centuries, empires have fallen and the world has transformed, yet the spirit of Kilcloher remains remarkably unchanged. The moss-covered ruins and ancient stone walls stand as silent witnesses to generations who lived, prayed, and found solace here. 

Today, visitors who travel to Kilcloher often remark on the profound peace that lingers over the land. In a world dominated by noise and constant motion, this sacred landscape offers a rare opportunity for stillness. Whether through the lens of faith, history, or a simple appreciation for nature, one cannot help but feel that in Kilcloher, the presence of God lives on in the very fabric of the earth, stone, and sky.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a narrative poem set in coastal Ireland about a boy who dies jumping off a cliff into the sea. Include details like curragh-men finding him, a priest denying him a Christian burial, and a compassionate figure named Argyle helping the family dig his grave while offering words of comfort.
counterfactuals.output:
Where wild Atlantic surges beat
Against the Irish stone,
Young Rory stood upon the cliff,
Unthinking and alone.
The wind was in his tangled hair,
The salt was on his breath;
A moment’s dare, a boyish leap
Between the sky and death.

He flew as birds fly toward the sun,
A silhouette of grace,
Then shattered on the icy green
In ocean’s harsh embrace.
The black tide took his fleeting breath
And swept him out from shore,
And where he plunged into the foam,
He rose to life no more.

At dusk, through thick and creeping fog,
The curragh-men came home,
Their tarred-cloth boats like shadows dark
Upon the churned-up foam.
They saw him tangled in the weed
Beneath the cliff’s cold wall,
And hauled his broken, heavy frame
From out the water's thrall.

They laid him on the shingled beach
Beside the crying tide;
His mother fell upon his breast,
His father knelt beside.
The fishermen bowed low their heads
And wiped the salt away,
Then bore him up the winding path
In twilight’s fading grey.

They brought him to the chapel gates
Before the night grew deep,
Hoping to lay their boy to rest
Where ancient ancestors sleep.
But there the parish priest stood tall,
His face as hard as stone,
He raised a dark and heavy hand
To leave the dead alone.

"No holy ground for such a act,"
The bitter priest declared.
"He threw away the gift of life;
His soul cannot be spared.
Unshriven, rash, he chose the deep—
I will not ring the bell.
Turn back, turn back! Beyond the wall
Is where his bones must dwell."

The mother wept in black despair,
The father hung his head,
Denied a cross, denied a prayer
To guard their precious dead.
To think their child must lie unblest
Beside the bitter sea,
Outcast from God and holy earth
For all eternity.

Then through the mist walked old Argyle,
A man of rugged hand,
Who knew the secrets of the tide
And lived upon the land.
He carried neither cross nor book,
But brought a sturdy spade,
And looked upon the grief-struck home
Unfrightened, undismayed.

"The earth is God’s," Argyle spoke low,
"Not bounded by a wall.
The sea, the turf, the sky above—
His mercy holds them all.
Come, bring the boy up to the crest
Where wild sea-pinks abide;
He’ll rest within the finest dirt
Above the turning tide."

Beneath the starlight's quiet veil,
Argyle drove in the blade.
Beside the father, hand in hand,
The lonely grave was made.
They dug through peat and moss and stone
To make his bedding deep,
While wind and wave played lullabies
To soothe the boy to sleep.

And as they lowered Rory down
Into the scented sod,
Argyle turned to the mother’s side
And spoke the peace of God:
"No priest can bar the gates of heaven,
No wall can keep Him out;
Your boy is safe in kinder arms
Than those who judge and doubt."

"The sea that caught him as he fell,
The cliff that saw him fly,
Are holy as an altar-rail
Beneath the open sky.
He did not leap from mercy’s reach,
Though men may turn away;
He sleeps within his native soil
Until the final day."

They filled the earth, they set a stone,
And Argyle bowed his head.
The ocean sang a solemn mass
Above the boy’s green bed.
And though no priest had blessed the ground,
The family felt no fear—
For love had made a hallowed place,
And God was standing near.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic poem exploring religious dogma versus human compassion following a tragedy in a traditional Irish fishing village.
counterfactuals.output:
The tide brought back young Liam’s coat today,
Tangled in kelp along the Barna Bay.
The sea is blind; it takes the bright, the wild,
And leaves a mother weeping for her child.
The salt hangs heavy in the turf-smoke air,
Where quiet women gather in despair,
Their aprons wet, their rosaries in hand,
To wait for what the waters wash to land.

By dusk they found him, pale beneath the moon,
Cut down before his blossom reached its June.
A lad who took the dark road in his head,
And let the ocean pull him to his bed.
And so the parish priest, in cassock black,
Stood at the chapel door and turned them back.

"Unsanctified," the solemn father said,
"The Church’s earth is not for such a dead.
He died in sin, by his own desperate hand,
He cannot sleep within this holy land."
He turned the key; the iron gates swung tight,
And left the boy to face the winter night.
For dogma keeps a cold and careful ledger,
And draws its lines along the graveyard fence.

The villagers stood silent in the rain,
Their faces etched with centuries of pain.
Old Manus, who had fished the bay for years,
Looked at the priest through eyes unwashed of tears,
Then spat upon the gravel, turned his cart,
And answered with a wild and human heart.

"If Heaven’s gates are barred by book and key,
Then we will build a altar by the sea."

They walked beyond the parish boundary wall,
Where yellow gorse and stubborn nettles fall,
Down where the cliffs look out toward the west,
To lay the boy they loved so well to rest.
No Latin prayers were read, no bells were rung,
No incense through the heavy air was swung,
Yet harbor men dug deep into the sod,
And held a quiet funeral with God.

A neighbor woman wrapped him in her shawl;
A fisherman let salty tear-drops fall.
They pressed a wooden cross into the earth,
And spoke of Liam’s kindness and his worth—
How he had hauled the nets when winter blew,
And shared the only bread his cabin knew.

And as the ocean hummed its ancient psalm,
The quiet headland settled into calm.
For grace was not in stone or Latin creed,
Nor in a dogma blind to human need,
But in the gentle hands that dug the clay,
To hide a broken boy from Barna Bay.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Could you compose a story-poem about a young boy who takes his own life off the cliffs of Kilcloher? Focus on the family's grief, the priest's cold refusal of a proper funeral, and a local named Argyle who reframes the tragic act as a "leap of faith."
counterfactuals.output:
The winds of Kilcloher blow dark on the stone,
Where the gray ocean batters the headland alone.
A pair of small boots was left quiet and still
Where the thrushes once sang on the rise of the hill,
And the village awoke to an infinite loss:
A lad who had carried an unseen, heavy cross.
He was only a boy, with the tide in his eyes,
Who stepped out of time 'neath the overcast skies.

His mother stood wailing her grief to the gales,
While the fishermen folded their useless, wet sails.
His father sat broken upon the dark shore,
Staring out at the waves that would yield him no more.
No note left behind, not a word to explain,
Just the terrible echo of unspoken pain,
And a void in the kitchen where laughter had played,
Now drowned in the depths of the choices he made.

They carried their heartbreak up Church Lane that night,
Seeking solace in scripture, and candle, and light.
To lay their sweet boy in the consecrated ground,
Where the rest of his kin in their slumber were bound.
But the priest stood impassive, a silhouette cold,
Guarding the gates of his rigid old fold.

"No holy earth waits for the soul that has bled
By its own desperate hand," was the judgment he said.
"No bell shall be tolled, and no mass shall be sung,
For the dark, mortal sin of a life ended young.
The law is the law, and the doctrine is clear;
I cannot bestow holy sacraments here."

The mother fell down on the frost-bitten gate,
Her boy turned away to a desolate fate.
The neighbors shrank back in their silence and dread,
Too frightened to pray for the unblessed dead.

Then out from the shadows stepped Argyle the old,
A man of the headlands, rugged and bold,
Whose skin was like driftwood, whose eyes held the sea,
Who walked where the wild winds blew untamed and free.
He lifted the father, he took the mother’s hand,
And led them away from the church on the land.

"Forget his cold gates and his books made of stone,"
Said Argyle softly, in a resonant tone.
"The boy is not damned, nor abandoned to night—
He was reaching for peace in the blinding sea-light.
Don't measure his heart by the priest's narrow rule,
Nor call him a sinner, nor call him a fool.

"When he stood on the brink where the sea-falcons soar,
And stepped off the edge from a life he could bear no more,
'Twas no act of ruin, nor a surrender to death—
It was a leap of pure faith on his very last breath.
He stepped into the air, casting sorrow behind,
Believing a mercy in the deep he would find.
He trusted the ocean, the wind, and the skies
To catch the sweet spirit that lived in his eyes."

They buried the lad on Kilcloher’s green crest,
Where the wild clover blooms and the storm-petrels rest.
No priest blessed the soil, but the ocean roared grand,
As Argyle placed heather in the grieving mother's hand.
And there on the cliffs, where the gray waters roll,
They left the sea wind to sing peace to his soul.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in modern narrative verse about a boy's drowning in rural Ireland, incorporating themes of judgment, redemption, and a non-traditional burial. Use Irish imagery like curraghs, estuary fishing, and coreligionists.
counterfactuals.output:
The estuary was a place of double currents,
where the brown peaty rush of the mountain river
met the green, cold thrust of the Atlantic tide.
Liam knew it by the smell of dulse and silt,
knew how to balance his weight in the curragh—
that light, black shell of tarred canvas and ash—
while dropping the drift-nets for salmon 
in the twilight between the salt-marsh and the deep.

It took only a snagged line, a sudden swell,
or perhaps the shifting weight of a sixteen-year-old boy
leaning too far into the twilight.
The curragh upturned like a floating beetle,
its belly dry in the drizzle while Liam went down
into the dark, brackish mixing of the waters,
his heavy woolen jumper dragging him into the mud.

They found him at dawn, wedged in the reeds by the spit.
His coreligionists gathered on the embankment,
hands jammed deep into the pockets of dark coats,
watching the water drain from his pale, quiet face.
Then came the quiet murmurings, the sharp, cold math of doctrine:
He had missed Mass that morning to check the nets.
He died without the last oil on his forehead,
without the priest’s Latin to bridge the gap.
And some whispered—because rural silence is always heavy with malice—
that a boy who goes into the water alone on a Sunday 
might have gone looking for the bottom.

The canon shook his head at the cemetery gates.
Rules were rules, written in distant Rome and kept in damp stone towns:
no suicides, no unabsolved souls within the consecrated wall.
He belonged outside, in the weed-choked ditch,
or in the forgotten *cillín* with the unbaptized infants.

So his father and his brother took him back.
Not to the cold damp clay of the parish yard,
and not to the ditch where the village cast its shames,
but out to the very mouth of the bay,
where the wind smelled of iodine and open sky.

By the light of a storm-lantern, they dug a grave
high on the sand-dune above the wrack line,
where the sea-holly grew wild and the bent-grass sang in the gale.
They laid him down in a shroud of gray sailcloth,
with a pocketful of gravel from the riverbed
and a sprig of dried heather from the hills.

No priest spoke above him, but the estuary roared its own liturgy.
The salt water crept up the sand at high tide to touch his feet,
a daily baptism that no man could deny or withhold.
Here, away from the narrow eyes of the righteous,
he was given over to the wind and the herring gulls,
 absolved not by words spoken over dust,
but by the vast, indifferent grace of the sea,
which takes every boy into its kingdom
and judges none of them.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a tragic narrative poem about a family mourning a suicide that the local church refuses to bless or bury in consecrated ground.
counterfactuals.output:
The parish bell refused to toll,
The church doors closed against the night.
They brought the body of the boy
Before the fading autumn light.
Young Thomas, barely twenty-one,
Who fought a war behind his eyes,
Had sought at last the quiet dark
Beneath the bitter November skies.

The priest stood tall upon the steps,
In cassock black and collar stiff,
His face set hard as winter slate,
Unmoving as a granite cliff.
"He took the breath that God had lent,
He broke the law, he crossed the line.
He died in sin, impenitent,
He cannot sleep in ground divine."

The mother fell upon her knees,
Her fingers clutching wet red clay,
"He was a child with broken wings!
Oh, Father, do not turn away!
The darkness stole his gentle mind,
It was a sickness, not a pride—
Have you no mercy in your heart
For how my poor boy lived and died?"

"The Canon stands," the priest replied,
And turned his back against her prayer.
The heavy oak doors shut and locked,
And left them in the biting air.
No incense rose, no psalm was sung,
No holy water touched his brow;
The iron bell remained unhung,
A silent judge above them now.

Beyond the churchyard’s carved stone wall,
Beyond the green and hallowed mound,
Where brambles choke the ditch in fall,
They bore him to the unblessed ground.
Outside the fence, where weeds grow wild,
Where thieves and nameless strangers lie,
They brought the gentle, shattered child
Beneath an unforgiving sky.

His father struck the freezing loam,
Each shovel full a jagged cry,
To dig his youngest son a home
Where holy feet would pass him by.
No priest was there to say the words,
No choir sang to ease their pain,
Save for the sorrow of the birds
And steady dripping of the rain.

The mother knelt beside the grave,
And pulled a faded linen shawl,
"If heaven sits behind that church,
Then God was never there at all.
For God knows well the soul's despair,
The heavy crushing of the mind;
He needs no priest to hear a prayer,
Nor walls to keep his love confined."

She sprinkled tears instead of grace,
His sister dropped a withered rose,
And covered up the quiet face
Before the winter night could freeze.
They raised no cross to mark the head,
Lest cruel hands should pull it down,
But loved him more than all the dead
Who slept within the holy town.

The church sat dark in candle-glow,
Where righteous men met to condemn,
While out where wild thistles grow,
The night draped soft its burial hem.
And softly fell the evening snow,
To blanket all the flinty sod,
And hold the boy the world cast out
Within the gentler arms of God.
